doubts.subject: DSA
doubts.author: Kabir Sethi
doubts.title: Why does my BST insert become O(n) on sorted input?

answers.author: Rohan Mehta
answers.body:
Your code is correct. The O(log n) claim is really "O(height)", and the height depends on the insertion order.

When you insert 1, 2, 3, ... in sorted order, every new key is bigger than everything already in the tree, so it always goes to the right:

```
1
 \
  2
   \
    3
     \
      4
       \
        5
```

With 5 nodes the height is 5, with 1000 nodes the height is 1000. Each insert walks the whole chain, so inserting n keys costs 1 + 2 + ... + n = O(n^2) and a single insert is O(n). This shape is called a degenerate tree.

Ways to fix it:
- Use a self-balancing tree. AVL and Red-Black trees rotate after inserts so the height stays O(log n). In Java, `TreeMap` is a Red-Black tree.
- If the input is known up front, shuffle it before inserting. Random order gives an expected height of about 1.39 log2 n.
- For a one-time build from sorted data, pick the middle element as the root and recurse on both halves.

So the claim "BST insert is O(log n)" holds only for balanced trees. For a plain BST the worst case is O(n).

answers.author: Navya Iyer
answers.body:
Adding to the above: you can see this yourself by writing a small `height(Node)` method and printing it after inserting 1..1000 in order and then in a shuffled order. Sorted gives 1000, shuffled gives something around 20 to 25. That difference is the whole point of balancing.

To get a feel for how bad it is: 1000 sorted inserts cost about 500,000 node visits (1 + 2 + ... + 1000), while the shuffled order costs roughly 1000 x 10 = 10,000. That is a 50 times difference for only 1000 keys, and the gap grows with n. This is exactly why databases and standard libraries use balanced trees instead of plain BSTs.

doubts.subject: DSA
doubts.author: Karan Gill
doubts.title: How is the 0/1 knapsack DP table filled, and why iterate capacity backwards in the 1D version?
doubts.body:
I understand the recursive idea for 0/1 knapsack (take the item or skip it) but the table filling is confusing me. Our teacher showed dp[i][w] for the 2D version and then said "to save space use a 1D array but loop the capacity from W down to the weight". I do not get why backwards. When I loop forwards, my answer for the same input becomes bigger than the 2D answer.

Example I am practising: items (weight, value) = (1,1), (3,4), (4,5), (5,7) and capacity W = 7. 2D table gives 9 as the answer.

Can someone explain the transition and the reason for the backward loop? This is for my mid-sem on Saturday.

answers.author: Rohan Mehta
answers.body:
Let dp[i][c] be the best value using only the first i items with capacity c. For item i with weight w and value v:

```
dp[i][c] = dp[i-1][c]                       if c < w
dp[i][c] = max(dp[i-1][c], dp[i-1][c-w] + v) if c >= w
```

Skip the item, or take it and add v to the best value for the remaining capacity c - w from the previous row. For your example the last row is `[0, 1, 1, 4, 5, 7, 8, 9]`, so dp[4][7] = 9 (the items of weight 3 and 4).

Each row depends only on the previous row, so you can keep one array. The catch is the order. dp[c] needs the OLD value of dp[c - w], the value from row i-1.

- Looping c upwards: when you reach c, dp[c - w] has already been updated for item i, so you may use the same item twice. That is the unbounded knapsack, which is why your answer becomes larger.
- Looping c downwards: dp[c - w] is at a smaller index and has not been touched yet in this round, so it still holds row i-1. Each item is used at most once.

```java
for (int i = 0; i < n; i++)
    for (int c = W; c >= wt[i]; c--)
        dp[c] = Math.max(dp[c], dp[c - wt[i]] + val[i]);
```

Time is O(nW) in both versions, space drops from O(nW) to O(W).

answers.author: Sneha Pillai
answers.body:
A quick check you can run on your own example: use one item (weight 3, value 4) and capacity 6. Going backwards gives dp[6] = 4 because the item is taken once. Going forwards gives dp[6] = 8 because the item gets counted twice. If you can see that, you understand the backward loop.

You can also print the dp array after each item for your example. After the first item (1,1) it is [0,1,1,1,1,1,1,1]. After (3,4) it becomes [0,1,1,4,5,5,5,5], which matches the 2D rows exactly. If your printed row ever differs from the 2D table, the loop direction is the first thing to check.

doubts.author: Arjun Malhotra
doubts.title: Detect a cycle in a singly linked list: why do the slow and fast pointers always meet?
doubts.body:
For the lab I have to detect a loop in a linked list without using extra memory. I found Floyd's tortoise and hare method online. Slow moves one step, fast moves two steps, and if they meet there is a cycle. The code makes sense but I do not understand why they must meet. Fast could jump over slow, right? Like if slow is at node 5 and fast is at node 4 they will swap places and miss each other?

Also sir asked us to find the node where the cycle starts. I cannot see how to get that from the meeting point.

answers.author: Rohan Mehta
Vikram Sandhu
answers.body:
Space is O(1) and time is O(n): slow enters the cycle after a steps and the gap closes within L more steps, so the total is at most a + L steps. Just remember the null check on `fast.next`, otherwise you crash on lists without a cycle.

To test your code, try three lists: an empty list, a single node pointing to itself, and a list where the last node points back to the second node. Print the node where the cycle starts for each. Also try a long list with no cycle, such as 1 to 100000, to confirm that fast reaches null and the loop ends in linear time.

doubts.subject: DSA
doubts.author: Gurnoor Dhillon
doubts.title: My binary search goes into an infinite loop sometimes

answers.author: Ishaan Gupta
Rohan Mehta
answers.body:
One thing to remember: the loop condition and the updates go together. `while (low <= high)` pairs with `mid + 1` and `mid - 1`. The other style, `while (low < high)` with `high = mid`, needs the lower mid and `low = mid + 1`. Mixing the two styles is what creates infinite loops, so pick one and stay with it.

To test it, run your function on arrays of size 0, 1 and 2, and with a key smaller than every element and larger than every element. These edge cases are where almost every binary search bug shows up, and a loop that handles all of them correctly is very likely right for the general case too.

doubts.subject: DSA
doubts.author: Dev Khanna
doubts.title: BFS vs DFS: which one gives the shortest path in an unweighted graph?
doubts.body:
Quiz question in our class: "Which traversal should be used to find the shortest path between two nodes in an unweighted graph?" I answered DFS because I find it easier to code, and I lost marks. The explanation said BFS but I did not get it.

DFS also reaches the target node, right? And it also finds a path. So why is the path from DFS not the shortest? Can someone explain with a small example? Also how do I recover the actual path and not just the distance?

answers.author: Rohan Mehta
Navya Iyer
answers.body:
A way to remember it: BFS expands in rings around the source, so the first ring that touches the target gives the shortest distance. DFS dives down one branch and commits to whatever it finds first.

On weighted graphs the same idea needs a priority queue instead of a plain queue, which is Dijkstra's algorithm. A good exam answer mentions all three cases: BFS for unweighted shortest paths in O(V + E), Dijkstra for non-negative weights in O((V + E) log V), and Bellman-Ford when negative edges are present. Knowing when each one applies earns the marks.

doubts.subject: DSA
doubts.author: Siddharth Jain
doubts.title: Infix to postfix: my stack gives the wrong order for a - b - c
doubts.body:
I wrote infix to postfix conversion using a stack for the lab. It works for a + b * c, which gives abc*+. But a - b - c gives abc-- instead of ab-c-. My code pops operators only when the stack top has strictly greater precedence than the current operator. Then I tried a ^ b ^ c and the textbook says the answer is abc^^, which looks like what I get.

So the same rule works for one case and breaks another. What exactly is the rule for operators with equal precedence?

answers.author: Rohan Mehta
answers.body:
The rule depends on associativity.

- For left-associative operators (+, -, *, /): pop while the top of the stack has precedence greater than OR EQUAL to the current operator. So in `a - b - c`, when the second `-` arrives the stack holds `-`, which is equal, so you pop it first. Output: `ab-c-`, which means (a - b) - c.
- For right-associative operators (^ and assignment): pop only while the top has strictly greater precedence. So in `a ^ b ^ c`, the second `^` does not pop the first, and the result is `abc^^`, which means a ^ (b ^ c).

Your code uses "strictly greater" for everything. That is correct for `^` but wrong for `-`.

```java
while (!st.isEmpty() && st.peek() != '('
       && (prec(st.peek()) > prec(c)
           || (prec(st.peek()) == prec(c) && isLeftAssoc(c))))
    out.append(st.pop());
st.push(c);
```

Test with `a-b-c` (expect `ab-c-`) and `a^b^c` (expect `abc^^`). Also remember to pop everything left on the stack at the end, and treat `(` and `)` separately.

answers.author: Vikram Sandhu
answers.body:
If you evaluate your postfix output with a second stack you can catch this bug automatically. Evaluate `abc--` with a=9, b=5, c=2: you get 9 - (5 - 2) = 6, but the infix 9 - 5 - 2 is 2. A mismatch like that tells you the conversion is wrong.

Also check parentheses before submitting: for (a + b) * c the output should be ab+c*, which means the opening bracket must stay on the stack until its matching closing bracket arrives, and then everything above it is popped. Missing that case is the second most common bug in this lab.

doubts.subject: DSA
doubts.author: Kabir Sethi
doubts.title: Is O(n log n) always faster than O(n^2)? My test with n = 10 says otherwise
doubts.body:
We learned that merge sort is O(n log n) and bubble sort is O(n^2) so merge sort should always be faster. But I timed both on an array of 10 numbers and bubble sort finished first. Then I tried 100 and merge sort still did not win by much.

Is my code wrong or is O(n log n) not always faster? What does Big-O really promise?

answers.author: Tanvi Rao
answers.body:
Big-O is an asymptotic statement: "for large enough n, the n log n algorithm wins". It does not say where "large enough" starts. Real running time includes constants. Say merge sort costs 100 * n * log2(n) operations (allocation, copying) and bubble sort costs n * n.

- n = 10: merge sort 3,322 versus bubble 100. Bubble wins easily.
- n = 100: 66,439 versus 10,000. Bubble still wins.
- n = 1000: about 996,578 versus 1,000,000. They are almost equal.
- Beyond n of about 1000, merge sort wins and the gap keeps growing.

That is why library sorts such as Java's TimSort switch to insertion sort for small chunks. So your code is not wrong. Test with n = 100,000 and you will see the difference.

hints.content: Big-O describes how running time grows as n becomes very large. Does it say anything about the constants hidden behind the notation, or about small n?

**Approach**
- Big-O drops constant factors and lower-order terms, so a real running time looks like `c1 * n log n + overhead` versus `c2 * n^2`.
- Compare the two functions at different values of n, using realistic constants (merge sort allocates and copies arrays, bubble sort only swaps in place).
- Find the crossover point where the n log n curve finally drops below the n^2 curve.
- Pitfall: timing tiny inputs mostly measures start-up cost and cache effects, not the algorithm.

doubts.subject: DSA
doubts.author: Gurnoor Dhillon
doubts.title: Reverse the words in a string in place, but my output has extra spaces
doubts.body:
Lab question: reverse the order of words in a string, like "the sky is blue" becomes "blue is sky the". We are supposed to do it in place using a char array. My idea was to reverse the whole string and then reverse each word. It works when words are separated by exactly one space but if the input has extra spaces at the start or end, the output also has them in the wrong places.

How should I handle the extra spaces without using split()?

hints.content: Your reverse-all-then-reverse-each-word idea is right. Ask yourself: what should happen to the spaces before you reverse any word, so that the reversal step only ever sees single spaces?

**Approach**
- Step 1: clean the spaces first with a two-pointer pass (a read index and a write index): skip leading spaces, copy letters, and write at most one space between words, then drop the trailing one.
- Step 2: reverse the cleaned range completely.
- Step 3: walk through it again and reverse each word between spaces.
- Pitfall: remember to use the new length after cleaning, not the original length, when you reverse.

doubts.subject: DSA
doubts.author: Karan Gill
doubts.title: Why is quicksort O(n^2) in the worst case and when does it happen?
doubts.body:
Everyone says quicksort is fast in practice, but my notes say worst case O(n^2). I do not understand how a divide and conquer algorithm can become quadratic. In the exam they will probably ask for the input that causes the worst case. I am using the last element as pivot in my code.

Please also explain what the average case looks like and why choosing a random pivot helps. I will be solving previous year questions on this tomorrow.

hints.content: Think about what a "good" partition looks like and what a "bad" one looks like. If the pivot is the last element and the array is already sorted, where does the pivot end up after partitioning, and how big are the two sides?

**Approach**
- Write the recurrence for a bad split: one side has n-1 elements and the other has 0, so T(n) = T(n-1) + O(n).
- Unroll it to see the sum n + (n-1) + ... + 1.
- Identify which inputs cause this with a last-element pivot (sorted or reverse sorted arrays, or all equal keys with a naive partition).
- Compare with the balanced split T(n) = 2T(n/2) + O(n).
- Pitfall: random pivot or median-of-three makes the bad case very unlikely.

doubts.subject: DSA
doubts.author: Siddharth Jain
doubts.title: Deleting a BST node with two children: inorder successor or predecessor, does it matter?
doubts.body:
Our textbook deletes a node with two children by replacing it with the inorder successor (smallest in the right subtree). My friend's notes use the inorder predecessor (largest in the left subtree). Both seem to work on the examples I tried.

Are both correct? Is one of them better? Also I keep making a mistake after copying the successor's value: I forget to delete the successor node and then I have duplicate keys in the tree.

answers.author: Navya Iyer
answers.body:
Both are correct. The BST property needs the replacement key to be larger than everything in the left subtree and smaller than everything in the right subtree. The inorder successor is the smallest key in the right subtree, so it satisfies that. The inorder predecessor is the largest key in the left subtree, and it satisfies it too.

The successor always has no left child (otherwise there would be a smaller key), so removing it is easy: it has at most one child, on the right. The predecessor has no right child for the same reason.

The procedure, using the successor:
1. Find the successor: go to the right child, then keep going left.
2. Copy its key into the node you are deleting.
3. Delete the successor from the right subtree. This is a recursive call to delete(root.right, successorKey), and it is the step you forgot.

Choice does not change the complexity (O(h)). Some implementations alternate between the two to keep the tree from leaning to one side over many deletions.

answers.author: Sneha Pillai
answers.body:
Your duplicate key bug is the classic one. After copying the key you must remove the original successor node, otherwise the same key stays in the tree. A good test is to delete the root from a tree of 7 nodes and print the inorder traversal. It must stay sorted with no repeated values.

For practice, delete the root from the tree built by inserting 50, 30, 70, 20, 40, 60, 80. The inorder successor of 50 is 60, so 60 replaces 50 and the old leaf 60 is removed. Doing the predecessor version (40) on the same tree and comparing the two shapes is a good exercise for the lab viva.

doubts.subject: DSA
doubts.author: Arjun Malhotra
doubts.title: Dijkstra gives a wrong answer with a negative edge, but sir said it works if there is no negative cycle
doubts.body:
Our teacher said "Dijkstra fails with negative edges" in one lecture and "it is fine as long as there is no negative cycle" in the revision class. I am confused which one is right. I tried a small graph: s -> a with weight 2, s -> b with weight 3, b -> a with weight -2. There is no negative cycle. Dijkstra from s gives dist(a) = 2 but I can reach a with cost 3 + (-2) = 1.

Did I implement Dijkstra wrongly or is the statement wrong?

answers.author: Vikram Sandhu
answers.body:
Your implementation is fine. The statement "Dijkstra works if there is no negative cycle" is not true for the standard algorithm.

Dijkstra is greedy. When it takes the closest unvisited node out of the priority queue, it assumes no later path can be shorter, because all edge weights are non-negative and extending a path can only add cost. With a negative edge, that assumption breaks.

On your graph: from s, a has distance 2 and b has 3. Dijkstra picks a (distance 2) and finalises it. Later it reaches b and relaxes b -> a to 1, but a is already finalised, so the better value is never used. The correct answer for a is 1.

Options:
- Bellman-Ford handles negative edges and detects negative cycles, in O(VE).
- For a DAG, relax edges in topological order in O(V + E).
- A variant of Dijkstra that lets nodes re-enter the queue gives correct results with negative edges (but no negative cycles), though its worst case is exponential. That is probably what sir meant, but it is not the standard algorithm.

doubts.subject: DSA
doubts.author: Kabir Sethi
doubts.title: Climbing stairs recursion is too slow for n = 45. How does memoization change it?

answers.author: Tanvi Rao
Ishaan Gupta
answers.body:
You can also do it bottom-up with two variables, which is O(n) time and O(1) space: keep `prev` and `curr` and update them in a loop. It is the same idea as printing Fibonacci numbers. Top-down memoization is easier to derive, and bottom-up saves the recursion stack.

Another way to present the answer in an exam is through the state: ways(i) depends only on ways(i-1) and ways(i-2). Because only two previous values matter, you can drop the array completely. That is the standard space optimisation for one-dimensional DP problems like this one, and the same trick works for the house robber problem.

doubts.subject: DBMS
doubts.author: Dev Khanna
doubts.title: How do I check if a relation is in BCNF when there are two candidate keys?
doubts.body:
We have a mid-sem on normalization and this question from the past paper is confusing me. Relation R(A, B, C, D) with functional dependencies:

AB -> C
C -> A
AB -> D

Sir said first find all candidate keys and then check every FD. I found AB as a key, but my friend says there are two candidate keys. How do I find all of them? And how do I decide whether the relation is in BCNF? If it is not, how do I decompose it, and is the decomposition lossless?

answers.author: Rohan Mehta
answers.body:
Step 1: candidate keys. Compute closures.
- AB+ = {A, B, C, D} because AB -> C and AB -> D. So AB is a key.
- BC+: C -> A gives A, so we have {B, C, A}; then AB -> D gives D. BC+ = {A, B, C, D}, so BC is also a key.
- Any key needs B, because B appears on no right-hand side. A and C alone cannot work, and no single attribute is a key, so the candidate keys are AB and BC.

Step 2: BCNF check. For every non-trivial FD X -> Y, X must be a superkey.
- AB -> C: AB is a key. OK.
- AB -> D: OK.
- C -> A: C+ = {C, A}, which is not all attributes, so C is not a superkey. Violation. The relation is NOT in BCNF. (It is in 3NF, since A is a prime attribute.)

Step 3: decompose using the violating FD C -> A.
- R1(C, A), with FD C -> A. C is a key of R1.
- R2(B, C, D): R minus the attribute A, keeping C as the link. Here BC is a key, so BC -> D holds and it is in BCNF.

Lossless check: R1 and R2 share only C, and C -> A means C is a key of R1, so R1 join R2 gives back R exactly. Note that AB -> C is not preserved by this decomposition. BCNF decomposition is always lossless but may lose dependencies; that is the price versus 3NF.

answers.author: Simran Kaur
answers.body:
A shortcut for the exam: write the closure of the left side of every FD. If any closure is not the full attribute set (and the FD is non-trivial), you already have a BCNF violation. Do the key-finding only when you need it for the 3NF check, where prime attributes matter. Here C+ = {C, A} settles it in one line.

Also note the difference between being in BCNF and being dependency preserving: the decomposition (C, A) and (B, C, D) is lossless, but the FD AB -> C cannot be checked on either table alone. Examiners often ask this follow-up, so mention it in your answer.

doubts.subject: DBMS
doubts.author: Karan Gill
doubts.title: Difference between 3NF and BCNF: when can a relation be in 3NF but not in BCNF?
doubts.body: I know BCNF is stricter than 3NF but I cannot come up with an example where a relation is in 3NF and not in BCNF. In class sir said "3NF allows a dependency X -> A if A is a prime attribute". I understand the sentence but not the example. Please give a small relation with FDs that is in 3NF but not BCNF, and explain why 3NF allows it.

answers.author: Rohan Mehta
answers.body:
Take R(A, B, C) with FDs: AB -> C and C -> B.

Candidate keys: AB+ = {A, B, C}, so AB is a key. AC+: C -> B gives B, so AC+ = {A, B, C} and AC is a key too. So the keys are AB and AC, and the prime attributes are A, B and C (every attribute appears in some key).

Check the FDs:
- AB -> C: AB is a superkey. Fine for both forms.
- C -> B: C is not a superkey, so this violates BCNF. But in 3NF the rule is "X is a superkey OR the right side A is a prime attribute". B is prime, so 3NF accepts it.

So the relation is in 3NF but not in BCNF.

Why does 3NF allow it? 3NF was designed so that a lossless, dependency-preserving decomposition always exists. BCNF cannot always give you that. Decomposing this relation into (C, B) and (A, C) is lossless, but the FD AB -> C can no longer be checked inside a single table. So 3NF accepts a little redundancy (B repeated for every row with the same C) to keep dependencies enforceable.

answers.author: Simran Kaur
answers.body:
A real-life version of the same shape: a table (Student, Subject, Teacher) where each teacher teaches only one subject and each student has one teacher per subject. Teacher -> Subject violates BCNF because Teacher is not a key, but it is still in 3NF since Subject is a prime attribute.

To spot this in the exam, check each FD for the BCNF violation first. If a left side is not a superkey, look at the right side: if every attribute on it belongs to some candidate key (is prime), the relation is still in 3NF. Doing it in this order makes questions on 3NF versus BCNF take under a minute.

doubts.subject: DBMS
doubts.author: Karan Gill
doubts.title: Finding all candidate keys for R(A,B,C,D,E) with A->B, BC->E, ED->A
doubts.body:
Past paper question: R(A, B, C, D, E) with FDs A -> B, BC -> E, ED -> A. Find all candidate keys.

I started with attributes that do not appear on any right side. C and D never appear on the right, so every key must contain CD. CD+ is only {C, D} so I need to add more. I tried adding A and got ACD but I am not sure it is minimal and I do not know how to systematically find the others. I got 2 keys in the exam but I think there are 3.

answers.author: Rohan Mehta
answers.body:
Your start is right: C and D appear on no right-hand side, so every candidate key must contain CD. Then try adding each remaining attribute (A, B, E) one at a time and take closures.

- CD + A: ACD+. A -> B gives B, then BC -> E gives E. So ACD+ = {A, B, C, D, E}. Key.
- CD + B: BCD+. BC -> E gives E, then ED -> A gives A. So BCD+ = {A, B, C, D, E}. Key.
- CD + E: CDE+. ED -> A gives A, then A -> B gives B. So CDE+ = all. Key.

Each of these is minimal: removing any one attribute breaks it. For example, AD+ = {A, B, D} and AC+ = {A, B, C, E} (no D), and CD+ is only {C, D}. Since they all contain CD and differ in the third attribute, none contains another.

So there are three candidate keys: ACD, BCD and CDE. That is why you saw 3 in your head: you found ACD but must also try B and E as the third attribute.

Every attribute appears in some key, so all attributes are prime. Then the relation is in 3NF automatically (a relation whose attributes are all prime is always in 3NF).

answers.author: Ira Kapoor
answers.body:
Systematic method to remember: (1) attributes that never appear on the right must be in every key, (2) attributes that appear only on the right are in no key, (3) for the rest, add one attribute at a time to the mandatory set and test closures, then try pairs only if singles fail. Keep a note of the keys found so you can skip any set that contains one of them.

Finish by writing the keys as a set, {ACD, BCD, CDE}, so the examiner can see that you checked every combination and not only the first one you found.

doubts.subject: DBMS
doubts.author: Dev Khanna
doubts.title: Conflict serializable vs view serializable: how do I draw the precedence graph?
doubts.body: I have a schedule S: r1(A) r2(A) w1(A) w2(A) and the question asks whether it is conflict serializable. I know we draw a precedence graph and check for a cycle, but I do not know which pairs of operations give an edge. I also do not understand when a schedule is view serializable but not conflict serializable. Sir mentioned blind writes but I did not follow. Please explain with an example.

answers.author: Rohan Mehta
answers.body:
Two operations conflict if they belong to different transactions, touch the same data item, and at least one is a write. So the conflicting pairs are read-write, write-read and write-write. For each conflicting pair where Ti's operation comes first, draw an edge Ti -> Tj.

Your schedule S: r1(A) r2(A) w1(A) w2(A).
- r1(A) before w2(A): edge T1 -> T2.
- r2(A) before w1(A): edge T2 -> T1.
- w1(A) before w2(A): edge T1 -> T2 (again).
The graph has T1 -> T2 and T2 -> T1, which is a cycle. So S is NOT conflict serializable.

View serializability is weaker. Two schedules are view equivalent if (1) each transaction reads the same initial or written values, and (2) the final write on each item is by the same transaction. Example: S' = r1(A) w2(A) w1(A) w3(A).
- The precedence graph has T1 -> T2 (r1 before w2) and T2 -> T1 (w2 before w1): a cycle, so it is not conflict serializable.
- But compare with the serial order T1, T2, T3: T1 reads the initial A in both, and T3 makes the final write in both. They are view equivalent, so S' is view serializable.

The writes by T2 and T1 that nobody reads are "blind writes". Every conflict serializable schedule is view serializable, but not the other way around.

answers.author: Simran Kaur
answers.body:
Exam tip: view serializability testing is NP-complete, so questions are usually small. For anything with only reads before writes by the same transaction (no blind writes), conflict and view serializability give the same answer, so just draw the precedence graph and look for a cycle.

If the schedule has more than two transactions, list the edges in a table first (the pair of operations and the reason) and only then draw the graph. It prevents missed edges. Remember that an acyclic graph gives you an equivalent serial order through a topological sort, and that is often asked as a follow-up: give an equivalent serial schedule.

doubts.subject: DBMS
doubts.author: Aanya Sharma
doubts.title: Difference between WHERE and HAVING? I get an error when I use COUNT in WHERE
doubts.body:
For the SQL lab I wrote this query to list departments that have more than 5 employees:

```sql
SELECT dept_id, COUNT(*)
FROM employee
WHERE COUNT(*) > 5
GROUP BY dept_id;
```

It gives an error saying aggregate functions are not allowed in WHERE. My friend says to use HAVING instead but when I read about HAVING it looks the same as WHERE to me. What is the actual difference, and when do I use which one? This is for the lab evaluation on Monday.

answers.author: Riya Chopra
answers.body:
They filter at different stages of the query:

- WHERE filters individual rows BEFORE grouping. The aggregate values do not exist yet at that point, which is why COUNT(*) is not allowed there.
- HAVING filters whole groups AFTER GROUP BY has formed them, so it can use aggregates.

The logical order is: FROM -> WHERE -> GROUP BY -> HAVING -> SELECT -> ORDER BY.

Your corrected query:

```sql
SELECT dept_id, COUNT(*) AS emp_count
FROM employee
GROUP BY dept_id
HAVING COUNT(*) > 5;
```

You can use both together: first remove rows you do not want, then filter groups.

```sql
SELECT dept_id, AVG(salary)
FROM employee
WHERE status = 'ACTIVE'        -- row filter, before grouping
GROUP BY dept_id
HAVING AVG(salary) > 50000;    -- group filter, after grouping
```

Rule of thumb: if the condition mentions an aggregate (COUNT, SUM, AVG, MIN, MAX), it belongs in HAVING. Otherwise put it in WHERE, because filtering early is faster.

answers.author: Zoya Khan
answers.body:
Small addition: a condition on a plain column such as dept_id can technically go in HAVING when that column is in GROUP BY, but it is better in WHERE because it removes rows before the grouping work. The database does less work, and your query reads more clearly to the examiner.

In MySQL you can sometimes use the SELECT alias inside HAVING, but PostgreSQL does not allow it and standard SQL does not guarantee it. To be safe in the lab evaluation, repeat the aggregate expression in HAVING instead of using the alias.

answers.author: Ira Kapoor
answers.body:
Practice question to test yourself: list the departments whose average salary is above the company-wide average salary. You need HAVING for the group condition and a subquery for the company average, like HAVING AVG(salary) > (SELECT AVG(salary) FROM employee). If that makes sense, you understand HAVING.

The full query would look like this: SELECT dept_id, AVG(salary) FROM employee GROUP BY dept_id HAVING AVG(salary) > (SELECT AVG(salary) FROM employee). The subquery runs once and gives one number, which every group is compared with. Try it on a small table of five rows first, so you can verify the output by hand.

doubts.subject: DBMS
doubts.author: Karan Gill
doubts.title: How do I find the height of a B+ tree for 1 million records with a 4 KB block?
doubts.body:
Question from the DBMS tutorial sheet: block size 4096 bytes, search key 8 bytes, block pointer 8 bytes, 1,000,000 records indexed by a B+ tree. Find the order of the tree and the number of levels (height) needed.

I know an internal node with p pointers has p - 1 keys. I think the formula is 8p + 8(p - 1) <= 4096 but then I get stuck on how to find the number of leaf nodes and how many levels that gives. Do I use the minimum or maximum fill?

answers.author: Simran Kaur
answers.body:
Order of an internal node: p pointers and p - 1 keys must fit in one block.

8p + 8(p - 1) <= 4096, which gives 16p <= 4104, so p = 256 (since 16 * 257 = 4112 does not fit).

Leaf node: it holds key and record pointer pairs plus one pointer to the next leaf. With q pairs: 16q + 8 <= 4096, so q = 255.

Number of levels:
- Leaf level, with full leaves: ceil(1,000,000 / 255) = 3,922 leaf nodes.
- Level above the leaves: each node points to up to 256 children, so ceil(3,922 / 256) = 16 nodes.
- Root: 16 children fit in one node, so 1 node.

That makes 3 levels: root, 16 internal nodes, 3,922 leaves. Searching costs 3 block reads, plus 1 to fetch the record.

For the worst case, assume nodes are only half full (a B+ tree guarantees at least half). Leaves hold about 128 keys, so about 7,813 leaves. Internal nodes hold at least 128 children, so ceil(7813 / 128) = 62 nodes, then ceil(62 / 128) = 1 root. That is still 3 levels. Even in the worst case, 1 million records need only 3 to 4 block accesses, which is why B+ trees are used for database indexes.

answers.author: Ira Kapoor
answers.body:
Check your answer using the quick estimate height = ceil(log_p(N)). With p = 256 and N = 1,000,000: 256^2 = 65,536 and 256^3 = 16,777,216, so you need 3 levels. If you get something very different, recheck the order calculation.

Remember that the answer depends on what the question defines. Some books count the pointer to the next leaf in the leaf size, others define order as the maximum number of children. If the question gives a formula or an example, follow that and write your assumption in one line. Marks are given for method, so the reasoning matters as much as the final number.

doubts.subject: DBMS
doubts.author: Dev Khanna
doubts.title: My LEFT JOIN returns fewer rows than I expect
doubts.body:
I have two tables: students(id, name) with 40 rows and enrollments(student_id, course, grade). I wrote a LEFT JOIN so that every student appears, even if they have no enrollment:

```sql
SELECT s.name, e.course
FROM students s
LEFT JOIN enrollments e ON e.student_id = s.id
WHERE e.course = 'DBMS';
```

I expected 40 rows, with NULL course for those not enrolled, but I only get the students enrolled in DBMS. It looks like an INNER JOIN. Why does the LEFT JOIN not keep the unmatched students?

answers.author: Zoya Khan
answers.body:
The cause is the WHERE clause. After the LEFT JOIN, students with no enrollment have e.course = NULL. The test NULL = 'DBMS' evaluates to UNKNOWN, and WHERE keeps only rows where the condition is TRUE. So all the unmatched rows disappear and you get inner join behaviour.

Move the condition into ON, so it decides which enrollments match, not which rows survive:

```sql
SELECT s.name, e.course
FROM students s
LEFT JOIN enrollments e
       ON e.student_id = s.id AND e.course = 'DBMS';
```

This returns all 40 students. Those enrolled in DBMS show the course, and everyone else shows NULL.

hints.content: Think about what value `e.course` has for a student with no enrollment after the LEFT JOIN, and what happens when WHERE tests `NULL = 'DBMS'`. Which rows survive that test?

**Approach**
- Write out the logical order: the join runs first and produces NULL-filled rows, then WHERE filters the result.
- Evaluate the condition `e.course = 'DBMS'` on a NULL row: the answer is unknown, not true, so the row is dropped.
- Decide where the course condition should live if you want to keep all students: in the ON clause of the join, not in WHERE.
- Pitfall: any WHERE condition on the right-hand table of a LEFT JOIN quietly turns it into an inner join, unless it also checks for IS NULL.

doubts.subject: DBMS
doubts.author: Karan Gill
doubts.title: Weak entity vs strong entity: how do I decide the key of a weak entity?
doubts.body: In ER modelling I understand that a strong entity has its own primary key. For a weak entity, like DEPENDENT of EMPLOYEE, my notes say it has a partial key and depends on the owner. I do not understand how its primary key is finally formed when I convert the ER diagram to tables, and how I should draw it.

hints.content: A weak entity cannot be identified by its own attributes alone. Ask yourself: if two employees each have a dependent called "Aman", what extra piece of information tells the two Amans apart?

**Approach**
- Identify the owner (strong) entity and the identifying relationship, drawn with a double diamond.
- Pick the partial key (discriminator) of the weak entity, drawn with a dashed underline. It is unique only among dependents of the same owner.
- Form the table: the primary key is the owner's primary key plus the partial key.
- Add the owner's key as a foreign key, with delete cascade, because a weak entity cannot exist without its owner.
- Pitfall: do not use the partial key alone as the primary key.

doubts.subject: DBMS
doubts.author: Dev Khanna
doubts.title: Wait-die vs wound-wait: how do the two deadlock prevention schemes differ?
doubts.body: Our notes list two deadlock prevention schemes based on timestamps: wait-die and wound-wait. I keep mixing them up. Both use the age of the transaction but I cannot remember who waits and who is aborted in each. Can someone give a clear example with two transactions T1 (older) and T2 (younger)? Also, do the aborted transactions restart with a new timestamp?

answers.author: Ananya Verma
answers.body:
Both schemes use the timestamp (a smaller timestamp means an older transaction). The difference is what happens when a transaction requests a lock held by another.

Wait-die (non-preemptive):
- Older requests a lock held by younger: the older WAITS.
- Younger requests a lock held by older: the younger DIES (aborts and restarts).

Wound-wait (preemptive):
- Older requests a lock held by younger: the older WOUNDS the younger, which means the younger is aborted and rolled back, and the older takes the lock.
- Younger requests a lock held by older: the younger WAITS.

With T1 older and T2 younger: if T1 wants an item T2 holds, wait-die makes T1 wait, wound-wait aborts T2. If T2 wants an item T1 holds, wait-die aborts T2, wound-wait makes T2 wait.

Neither scheme can deadlock, because in wait-die only older ones wait for younger ones, and in wound-wait only younger ones wait for older ones, so a cycle of waits is impossible. Restarted transactions keep their ORIGINAL timestamp, otherwise a transaction could be aborted repeatedly and starve.

answers.author: Ira Kapoor
answers.body:
Memory trick: in wait-die, the OLD one waits (old people wait calmly), the young one dies. In wound-wait, the old one wounds, the young one waits. The first word of the name tells you what the older transaction does.

A quick example with timestamps TS(T1) = 5 and TS(T2) = 10, so T1 is older. If T2 holds a lock and T1 asks for it, wait-die lets T1 wait, while wound-wait aborts T2. If T1 holds it and T2 asks, wait-die aborts T2 and wound-wait lets T2 wait. Put this as a small table in the exam.

doubts.subject: DBMS
doubts.author: Karan Gill
doubts.title: Relational algebra for 'students who enrolled in ALL courses': I am confused about division
doubts.body: Tutorial question: find the ids of students who have enrolled in every course offered. The relations are Enrolled(sid, cid) and Course(cid). My teacher says to use the division operator but the definition in the book is hard to follow. Can I solve it without division using only select, project, join, cross product and set difference? I would like to understand how it works.

answers.author: Simran Kaur
answers.body:
With division it is one line: pi_sid,cid(Enrolled) divided by pi_cid(Course). The result contains every sid that is paired with ALL cids of Course.

Without division, the idea is "find the students who are missing at least one course, and remove them":

1. All possible (student, course) pairs: AllPairs = pi_sid(Enrolled) x pi_cid(Course).
2. The pairs that actually exist are Enrolled. So the missing pairs are Missing = AllPairs - Enrolled.
3. Students with at least one missing course: Bad = pi_sid(Missing).
4. Answer = pi_sid(Enrolled) - Bad.

Written together: pi_sid(Enrolled) - pi_sid((pi_sid(Enrolled) x pi_cid(Course)) - Enrolled).

Quick check: if student 1 is enrolled in {c1, c2} and Course has {c1, c2}, AllPairs has (1,c1), (1,c2), both exist in Enrolled, so Missing is empty and student 1 stays. If student 2 is enrolled only in c1, then (2,c2) is missing, so student 2 is in Bad and is removed.

doubts.subject: DBMS
doubts.author: Dev Khanna
doubts.title: Why does the optimizer choose a hash join here and not a nested loop join?
doubts.body: I ran EXPLAIN on a query joining orders (about 2 million rows) with customers (about 50,000 rows) on customer_id. The plan shows a hash join, and our notes say nested loop join is the basic method. There is no index on orders.customer_id. Why did it choose a hash join, and when would nested loop be better? I would like to know the cost reasoning, not just the name.

answers.author: Zoya Khan
answers.body:
The optimizer compares estimated costs, usually measured in disk block accesses or row comparisons.

Let B(R) and B(S) be the number of blocks, R the smaller table (customers) and S the larger (orders).
- Block nested loop join: read R once, and for each block of R scan all of S. Cost is about B(R) + B(R) * B(S). With no index, it reads the large table once for every block of the small one, which is very expensive.
- Hash join: build an in-memory hash table on the smaller table (50,000 customers fits in memory) and stream the large table past it once. Cost is about B(R) + B(S), so each table is read once.
- Index nested loop would be good if orders.customer_id had an index and only a few customers were selected, since each lookup would be O(log n).

So with an equality join condition, no usable index and a build side that fits in memory, hash join wins by a wide margin.

Nested loop is better when one side is very small (say a few rows after a filter), when an index exists on the inner table, or when the join condition is not an equality (hash join needs equality). Merge join is attractive when both inputs are already sorted.

doubts.subject: DBMS
doubts.author: Aanya Sharma
doubts.title: 2NF vs 3NF: is a transitive dependency allowed in 2NF?
doubts.body: I am trying to learn the normal forms in order. I understand 1NF (atomic values) and I think I get partial dependency for 2NF. But for 3NF my notes say "no transitive dependency". If a table is already in 2NF, can it still have a transitive dependency like student_id -> dept_id and dept_id -> dept_name? And if yes, how do I fix it? I would like a small example to understand the exact difference between the two.

doubts.subject: DBMS
doubts.author: Karan Gill
doubts.title: Undo/redo logging: what do I do for committed and uncommitted transactions after a crash?
doubts.body: I am studying log based recovery with immediate database modification. After a crash, the log has records like <T1, start>, <T1, A, 100, 150>, <T2, start>, <T2, B, 20, 40>, <T1, commit>. The system restarts. I know there are redo and undo operations but I cannot remember which transaction needs which, and in what order the log is scanned. Also what is the purpose of a checkpoint here?

doubts.subject: OS
doubts.author: Yash Arora
doubts.title: Why does my producer-consumer code deadlock with two semaphores?

answers.author: Meher Bajwa
Simran Kaur
answers.body:
A good way to catch this in future: draw a table of who holds what and who waits for what. If you find a circle (producer holds mutex and wants empty, consumer holds nothing but wants mutex while the producer waits for the consumer), it is a deadlock. The fix is always to break the circle by acquiring locks in a consistent order.

Also test with several producers and consumers, not just one of each, and with a tiny buffer size such as N = 1. Deadlocks that stay hidden with one producer often appear immediately when the buffer is small, and it is a good habit before the lab evaluation.

doubts.subject: OS
doubts.author: Pooja Saini
doubts.title: Effective access time with a TLB: 90% hit ratio, 20 ns TLB, 100 ns memory
doubts.body:
Numerical from the sheet: a paging system uses a TLB. TLB access time is 20 ns, main memory access time is 100 ns and the TLB hit ratio is 90 percent. Find the effective memory access time (EAT).

The book answer is 130 ns but I get 118 ns. I calculated 0.9 x 20 + 0.1 x 100 + 100. I think I am missing something about what happens on a miss. How many memory accesses are needed when the page is not in the TLB?

answers.author: Ananya Verma
answers.body:
You need to count the TLB lookup on EVERY access, and the page table access on a miss.

- TLB hit (probability 0.9): you search the TLB (20 ns) and then access the data in memory (100 ns). Total = 20 + 100 = 120 ns.
- TLB miss (probability 0.1): you search the TLB (20 ns), find nothing, read the page table entry from memory (100 ns), then access the data (100 ns). Total = 20 + 100 + 100 = 220 ns.

EAT = 0.9 x 120 + 0.1 x 220 = 108 + 22 = 130 ns.

Your calculation added the TLB time only on the hit part and did not add the extra memory access for the page table on a miss. The common formula is:

EAT = h x (t_tlb + t_mem) + (1 - h) x (t_tlb + 2 x t_mem)

Some books assume the TLB lookup overlaps with something else or ignore it; the problem statement usually tells you. With a single-level page table a miss costs two memory accesses. With a two-level table it would cost three, and the EAT would become 0.9 x 120 + 0.1 x 320 = 140 ns.

answers.author: Meher Bajwa
answers.body:
Sanity check: the answer must lie between the best case (120 ns, all hits) and the worst case (220 ns, all misses). 130 is close to 120 because 90% of accesses are fast. If your answer falls outside that range, there is an error.

For multi-level paging or a TLB with different hit and miss costs, always draw the two cases as separate lines first (hit path and miss path), compute each total and only then weight them by the probabilities. This habit avoids missing the extra page-table access, which is the most common reason for a wrong EAT.

doubts.subject: OS
doubts.author: Yash Arora
doubts.title: Round robin with quantum 2: my average waiting time differs from the book
doubts.body:
Problem: processes P1, P2, P3, P4 arrive at times 0, 1, 2, 3 with burst times 5, 3, 1, 2. Scheduling is round robin with time quantum 2. Find the average waiting time.

I drew a Gantt chart but I am not sure where to put a process that arrives while another one is running. I put P2 behind P1 in the queue after P1's first slice, and then I lost track. The answer key says 4.5 but I get 5.25. Where do newly arrived processes go?

answers.author: Simran Kaur
answers.body:
Rule used in most textbooks: a process that arrives during a time slice enters the ready queue BEFORE the preempted process is placed back at the tail.

Simulate (quantum 2):
- t=0: queue [P1]. P1 runs 0-2 (3 left). During this, P2 (t=1) and P3 (t=2) arrive, so the queue is [P2, P3] and then P1 goes to the back: [P2, P3, P1].
- P2 runs 2-4 (1 left). P4 arrives at t=3, so the queue is [P3, P1, P4, P2].
- P3 runs 4-5 and finishes (burst 1).
- P1 runs 5-7 (1 left). Queue: [P4, P2, P1].
- P4 runs 7-9 and finishes.
- P2 runs 9-10 and finishes.
- P1 runs 10-11 and finishes.

Gantt: P1(0-2) P2(2-4) P3(4-5) P1(5-7) P4(7-9) P2(9-10) P1(10-11).

Completion times: P1=11, P2=10, P3=5, P4=9. Turnaround = completion - arrival: 11, 9, 3, 6. Waiting = turnaround - burst: P1 = 6, P2 = 6, P3 = 2, P4 = 4.

Average waiting time = (6 + 6 + 2 + 4) / 4 = 4.5. That matches the key.

Your 5.25 likely comes from placing the preempted process before the newly arrived ones. If your course uses the opposite convention, say so in the answer.

answers.author: Priya Nair
answers.body:
Always state the tie-breaking rule at the top of the answer in exams, because the result changes with it. Also verify with the identity: sum of waiting times = sum of turnaround times - sum of burst times = (11 + 9 + 3 + 6) - (5 + 3 + 1 + 2) = 29 - 11 = 18, which gives 4.5 on average.

If a process arrives exactly when a quantum ends, the usual convention is the same: the new arrival goes into the queue first, then the preempted process. State this convention in your answer.

doubts.subject: OS
doubts.author: Pooja Saini
doubts.title: Banker's algorithm: how do I find a safe sequence step by step?
doubts.body:
I have the standard example: 5 processes P0 to P4 and 3 resource types A, B, C with total instances 10, 5, 7. Allocation: P0 (0,1,0), P1 (2,0,0), P2 (3,0,2), P3 (2,1,1), P4 (0,0,2). Max: P0 (7,5,3), P1 (3,2,2), P2 (9,0,2), P3 (2,2,2), P4 (4,3,3). Available is (3,3,2).

Is the system in a safe state? I know the steps (Need = Max - Allocation, then Work and Finish arrays) but when I try to pick processes I get confused about which to choose first and whether the order I pick changes the answer.

answers.author: Meher Bajwa
answers.body:
Need = Max - Allocation:
P0 (7,4,3), P1 (1,2,2), P2 (6,0,0), P3 (0,1,1), P4 (4,3,1).

Start with Work = Available = (3,3,2) and Finish = false for all. Repeatedly pick any unfinished process whose Need <= Work. When it finishes, add its Allocation back to Work.

1. P0 (7,4,3) > (3,3,2). Not possible. P1 (1,2,2) <= (3,3,2). Pick P1. Work = (3,3,2) + (2,0,0) = (5,3,2).
2. P3 (0,1,1) <= (5,3,2). Pick P3. Work = (5,3,2) + (2,1,1) = (7,4,3).
3. P0 (7,4,3) <= (7,4,3). Pick P0. Work = (7,4,3) + (0,1,0) = (7,5,3).
4. P2 (6,0,0) <= (7,5,3). Pick P2. Work = (7,5,3) + (3,0,2) = (10,5,5).
5. P4 (4,3,1) <= (10,5,5). Pick P4. Work = (10,5,5) + (0,0,2) = (10,5,7).

All processes finished, so the state is SAFE with safe sequence <P1, P3, P0, P2, P4>.

The order you pick can differ. <P1, P3, P4, P0, P2> is also a safe sequence for this data. Different orders are possible, but if ANY complete order exists the state is safe. At the end Work must equal the total resources (10,5,7), which is a good check on your arithmetic.

answers.author: Ananya Verma
answers.body:
If the question then asks "can a request from P1 for (1,0,2) be granted?", check three things in order: Request <= Need, Request <= Available, then pretend to grant it (Available - Request, Allocation + Request, Need - Request) and run the safety algorithm again. Grant only if the new state is still safe.

In the exam, show a table with the columns Process, Need, Work before, Work after and Finish. It makes the safe sequence easy to verify, and examiners can award method marks even if one arithmetic slip happens. Also state that the safe sequence is not unique.

doubts.subject: OS
doubts.author: Aanya Sharma
doubts.title: Difference between a process and a thread? Can two threads share the stack?
doubts.body: The definitions in my notes look the same to me: "a thread is a lightweight process". In the viva I got asked what two threads of the same process share and what they do not share. I said everything is shared and the examiner did not look happy. Can someone clearly list what is shared and what is private? I am especially confused about the stack and the registers.

answers.author: Priya Nair
answers.body:
A process is a program in execution with its own address space. A thread is a unit of execution inside a process.

Threads of the same process share: the code (text) section, global and static data, the heap, open files and other OS resources such as signal handlers.

Each thread has its own: stack (local variables and return addresses), program counter, CPU register values and a thread id. This is why two threads can run the same function at the same time without overwriting each other's local variables.

So the answer to your question is that threads do NOT share the stack, although technically all stacks live in the same address space, so a buggy thread could access another's stack through a pointer.

Context switching between threads of one process is cheaper than between processes because no address-space switch is needed. The price is that shared heap and globals need locks.

hints.content: Imagine two threads running the same function at the same time in one program. If they both used the same stack, what would go wrong with their local variables and return addresses?

**Approach**
- Make two columns: what lives in the process (shared by all its threads) and what each thread must have on its own.
- Think about the memory regions: code, global data, heap, open files on one side; stack, program counter, registers on the other.
- Explain why the private items must be separate: each thread has its own execution state.
- Pitfall: threads share the heap, so shared data needs synchronization.

doubts.subject: OS
doubts.author: Pooja Saini
doubts.title: Internal vs external fragmentation: why does paging remove external fragmentation?
doubts.body:
I can recite the definitions of internal and external fragmentation but I mix up which technique causes which. In the exam they ask "why does paging remove external fragmentation but still have internal fragmentation?" and I cannot explain it properly. Please explain with a small example using numbers.

I also get confused because both terms sound similar, and my teacher used a figure with coloured boxes that I could not copy properly. The exam is on Thursday and this is a 5 mark question.

hints.content: Ask which of the two wastes memory INSIDE an allocated block, and which wastes memory BETWEEN allocated blocks. Then ask what size every allocation is in paging.

**Approach**
- Define the two terms by where the waste sits: inside an allocation versus in gaps between allocations.
- Take page size 4 KB and a process of 10 KB; count how many pages it needs and how much of the last page is unused.
- Explain why any free frame can serve any page, so scattered free frames are never "too small".
- Pitfall: the average internal waste is about half a page per process, so smaller pages waste less but need bigger page tables.

doubts.subject: OS
doubts.author: Yash Arora
doubts.title: SCAN vs C-SCAN: do I count the jump back in the total head movement?
doubts.body:
Disk has 200 cylinders (0 to 199). Request queue: 98, 183, 37, 122, 14, 124, 65, 67 and the head is at 53. I need to find the total head movement for SCAN and C-SCAN.

For SCAN, I assume the head goes towards 0 first. I got 236 for SCAN, which matches the book. For C-SCAN moving towards higher cylinders I got 382 including the jump from 199 to 0, but my friend says 183 and the book shows both versions in different places. Which one is correct and does the head go to the very end of the disk?

answers.author: Meher Bajwa
answers.body:
Both of your numbers are right; they answer slightly different questions.

SCAN (towards 0 first), the head must go to the end of the disk (cylinder 0) before reversing:
53 -> 37 -> 14 -> 0 -> 65 -> 67 -> 98 -> 122 -> 124 -> 183.
Movement = (53 - 0) + (183 - 0) = 53 + 183 = 236.

C-SCAN (towards higher cylinders first): service requests going up, continue to the last cylinder 199, jump back to 0, then service the rest going up.
53 -> 65 -> 67 -> 98 -> 122 -> 124 -> 183 -> 199 -> 0 -> 14 -> 37.
- Going up: (199 - 53) = 146.
- The return jump: 199 (from 199 to 0).
- Going up again: 37.
Total = 146 + 199 + 37 = 382 if the return jump is counted.

Many textbooks do not count the return jump because the head moves back without serving requests and it is considered fast. Then the total is 146 + 37 = 183.

So always read the question: if it says "total head movement", state your assumption. In an exam write both: "382 including the return seek, 183 excluding it". Also note that the textbook versions that stop at the last request instead of the disk end are LOOK and C-LOOK, which give different totals.

answers.author: Simran Kaur
answers.body:
For comparison, FCFS on the same queue gives 640 cylinders of head movement. SCAN with 236 and C-SCAN (183 without the jump) are far better. The reason C-SCAN is preferred in practice is that it gives more uniform waiting times, because requests at the edges are not served twice as often as those in the middle.

As a quick comparison for revision: FCFS gives 640, SCAN gives 236 and C-SCAN gives 382 including the return jump. SSTF would serve 65, 67, 37, 14, 98, 122, 124, 183 for a total of 236 as well. The numbers show why scheduling matters more as the queue grows.

doubts.subject: OS
doubts.author: Yash Arora
doubts.title: inode: how many blocks can a file have with 12 direct, 1 single and 1 double indirect pointer?
doubts.body:
Unix style inode question: block size is 4 KB, a disk block address is 4 bytes. The inode has 12 direct pointers, 1 single indirect and 1 double indirect pointer. What is the maximum file size?

I know a single indirect block points to a block full of addresses. But I do not know how many addresses fit in one block and how the double indirect counts. I wrote 12 + 1 + 1 = 14 blocks which is obviously wrong. How do I get the real number?

answers.author: Ananya Verma
answers.body:
Count how many data blocks each kind of pointer can reach.

A block holds 4096 / 4 = 1024 addresses.

- 12 direct pointers: 12 data blocks.
- 1 single indirect pointer: points to one block holding 1024 addresses, so 1024 data blocks.
- 1 double indirect pointer: points to a block of 1024 addresses, each of which points to a block of 1024 addresses, so 1024 x 1024 = 1,048,576 data blocks.

Total data blocks = 12 + 1024 + 1,048,576 = 1,049,612.

Maximum file size = 1,049,612 x 4 KB = 4,198,448 KB, which is about 4.004 GB. In bytes that is 4,299,210,752.

The double indirect pointer dominates, so a quick estimate is 1024^2 blocks x 4 KB = 4 GB. If a triple indirect pointer existed, you would add 1024^3 blocks, which is 4 TB more.

answers.author: Meher Bajwa
answers.body:
A related detail for the viva: the index blocks themselves also take space on disk. For a file of maximum size you would use 1 single indirect block, 1 double indirect first-level block and 1024 second-level blocks. They are overhead and are not counted in the maximum file size, but they matter if the question asks for disk blocks used.

So for the same inode layout, a bigger block size increases the maximum file size very quickly, because the addresses per block grow and the double indirect term grows with the square of that number. With 8 KB blocks and 4-byte pointers you get 2048 addresses per block, and the double indirect part alone covers 2048 squared blocks.

doubts.subject: OS
doubts.author: Pooja Saini
doubts.title: Peterson's solution: why is the turn variable needed if we already have flags?
doubts.body: Peterson's algorithm for two processes uses flag[2] and turn. Each process sets its flag to true to show it wants to enter, and then sets turn to the other process, and waits while the other's flag is true and it is the other's turn. I understand the code but not why the turn variable is needed. If both flags are enough to show intent, why do we need turn as well? What breaks if I remove it?

answers.author: Priya Nair
answers.body:
Each variable fixes a different problem.

Without turn (flags only): each process sets its flag and then waits while the other's flag is true. If both set their flags at the same time, each sees the other's flag and waits forever. That is a deadlock. Flags show who wants to enter but cannot break a tie.

Without flags (turn only): the processes are forced to alternate. P0 can enter only when turn = 0 and P1 only when turn = 1. If P1 does not want to enter at all, P0 waits for its turn forever after one entry. That violates progress, because a process outside its critical section blocks another.

With both: a process says "I want in" (flag) and then politely says "you go first" (turn = other). If both do this at the same moment, the value of turn is written last by one of them, and that decides who goes: the process that wrote turn last is the one that waits. The other sees either the flag false or turn pointing to itself and enters. So we get:
- Mutual exclusion: both cannot pass the wait condition together.
- Progress: no deadlock, and a process that does not want in does not block the other.
- Bounded waiting: after P0 leaves, it must set turn to P1 if it comes again, so it waits at most one turn.

doubts.subject: CN
doubts.author: Harsh Vardhan
doubts.title: CRC remainder for message 1101011011 with generator 10011
doubts.body:
Tutorial problem: find the CRC for the message 1101011011 using the generator polynomial x^4 + x + 1 (bits 10011). I know I must append zeros and divide using XOR but my long division keeps going wrong. Every time I get a different remainder. The key says 1110 and the transmitted frame should be 11010110111110.

Can someone show the division step by step and also tell me how the receiver checks the frame?

answers.author: Priya Nair
answers.body:
The generator 10011 has degree 4, so append 4 zeros to the message:

Dividend = 1101011011 0000 = 11010110110000.

Binary (mod 2) division uses XOR with no borrows. At each step, if the leading bit of the current window is 1, XOR the generator under it; if it is 0, just shift. Running the full division gives these intermediate values (after each XOR with 10011):

```
11010110110000
10011                 (XOR at position 0)
--------------
01001110110000
 10011                (XOR at position 1)
 --------------
00000010110000
      10011           (XOR at position 6)
      --------------
00000000101000
        10011         (XOR at position 8)
        --------------
00000000001110
```

The last 4 bits are the remainder: 1110.

Transmitted frame = message followed by the remainder = 1101011011 1110 = 11010110111110.

Receiver check: divide the whole received frame (11010110111110) by 10011 using the same XOR division. If the remainder is 0000, the frame is accepted as error free; any non-zero remainder means an error was detected.

CRC detects all single-bit errors, all burst errors of length up to 4 (the degree of the generator) and any odd number of bit errors when the generator has a factor (x + 1). It cannot detect errors that happen to be a multiple of the generator.

answers.author: Meher Bajwa
answers.body:
A mistake many people make is dividing the message without appending the zeros first, or appending the wrong number of zeros. The number of zeros is always one less than the number of bits in the generator. Another trick for the exam: write the dividend and XOR in columns exactly as above, so you do not lose your position.

It is also worth practising the polynomial form. The generator x^4 + x + 1 is 10011, and the message here, 1101011011, is x^9 + x^8 + x^6 + x^4 + x^3 + x + 1. Being able to convert between the two forms is often asked as a separate part of the question, and mistakes there lead to a wrong divisor.

doubts.subject: CN
doubts.author: Siddharth Jain
doubts.title: Subnetting 192.168.10.0/24 into 6 subnets: new mask and the range of each subnet
doubts.body: Question: a company has the network 192.168.10.0/24 and needs at least 6 subnets. Find the new subnet mask, the number of hosts per subnet and the network address, broadcast address and usable range for each subnet. I know the formula 2^n >= subnets but I am confused about how many bits to borrow and how to list the subnets. Also, are the first and last subnets usable? Our teacher said something about subnet zero.

answers.author: Priya Nair
answers.body:
Borrow bits from the host part. You need at least 6 subnets, and 2^2 = 4 is too few, 2^3 = 8 is enough. So borrow 3 bits.

- New prefix: /24 + 3 = /27.
- New mask: 255.255.255.224 (the last octet is 11100000 = 224).
- Host bits left: 5, so each subnet has 2^5 = 32 addresses and 32 - 2 = 30 usable hosts.
- Block size = 256 - 224 = 32.

The subnets (network - first host - last host - broadcast):
1. 192.168.10.0   - .1   to .30  - .31
2. 192.168.10.32  - .33  to .62  - .63
3. 192.168.10.64  - .65  to .94  - .95
4. 192.168.10.96  - .97  to .126 - .127
5. 192.168.10.128 - .129 to .158 - .159
6. 192.168.10.160 - .161 to .190 - .191

There are 8 subnets in total; the last two (.192 and .224) are spare.

About subnet zero: older classful rules did not allow the first (all zeros) and the last (all ones) subnet. Modern classless routing (CIDR) allows them, so with CIDR you can use all 8. If the question says "classful" or "subnet zero not allowed", you would need 2^3 - 2 = 6 usable subnets, which is exactly why this question asks for 6.

answers.author: Vikram Sandhu
answers.body:
Fast method to avoid mistakes: the interesting octet value is 224, so the block size is 256 - 224 = 32. Subnets start at multiples of 32. The broadcast is always the next network address minus 1. The usable range is network + 1 to broadcast - 1. Do this and you never need to convert to binary in the exam.

To verify your table, check that each broadcast address plus one equals the next network address, for example .31 + 1 = .32. If that holds for all rows, your block size and ranges are right, and the host count of 30 per subnet follows from 2^5 - 2.

doubts.subject: CN
doubts.author: Harsh Vardhan
doubts.title: Slow start vs congestion avoidance: how does cwnd change, and what happens on a timeout?
doubts.body: I am trying to draw the congestion window graph for TCP. Initial ssthresh is 16 MSS and cwnd starts at 1 MSS. I know cwnd doubles each RTT in slow start and then increases linearly. But I do not understand when exactly slow start ends, and what happens to cwnd and ssthresh when a timeout occurs at cwnd = 20. Is it different for a triple duplicate ACK?

answers.author: Vikram Sandhu
answers.body:
Slow start: cwnd starts at 1 MSS and doubles every RTT (it increases by 1 MSS for every ACK received): 1, 2, 4, 8, 16. When cwnd reaches ssthresh (16), slow start ends.

Congestion avoidance: cwnd increases by 1 MSS per RTT (additive increase): 17, 18, 19, 20, ...

Timeout at cwnd = 20 (this is a strong signal of congestion):
- ssthresh = cwnd / 2 = 10.
- cwnd = 1 MSS.
- Start slow start again: 1, 2, 4, 8, then 10 (it reaches ssthresh and switches to linear growth): 11, 12, ...

Triple duplicate ACK (a mild signal, because later segments are still getting through):
- TCP Tahoe treats it like a timeout: ssthresh = 10, cwnd = 1.
- TCP Reno uses fast retransmit and fast recovery: ssthresh = cwnd / 2 = 10, cwnd = ssthresh (+ 3 MSS during recovery) and continues in congestion avoidance, without dropping to 1.

So a timeout always resets cwnd to 1, but with Reno a triple duplicate ACK only halves it. This sawtooth, with additive increase and multiplicative decrease, is what AIMD means.

answers.author: Priya Nair
answers.body:
Plot tip for the exam: x-axis in RTTs, y-axis cwnd in MSS. Label the ssthresh line, mark the slow start region as exponential, the congestion avoidance region as a straight line, and the timeout as a vertical drop to 1. Examiners look for the new ssthresh being half of the cwnd at the time of loss, not half of the old ssthresh.

Also write down which TCP variant the question assumes. Tahoe and Reno differ only for triple duplicate ACKs, and many exam answers lose marks by not saying which version they used. When in doubt, mention both behaviours in one line.

doubts.subject: CN
doubts.author: Yash Arora
doubts.title: Distance vector count-to-infinity: why does it happen and how does split horizon fix it?
doubts.body: Our notes on distance vector routing mention the count-to-infinity problem. I read the example with three routers A - B - C in a line, where the link between B and C goes down, but I could not follow why the costs keep increasing. What exactly is exchanged and why do B and A keep updating? And how does split horizon help? Does it solve every case?

answers.author: Meher Bajwa
answers.body:
Setup: A - B - C in a line, all link costs 1. A's table says C is at distance 2 (via B), and B's table says C is at distance 1.

The B-C link fails. B no longer reaches C directly, but it hears from A that "C is at distance 2". B cannot know that A's route to C goes through B itself, so B believes A and sets C = 3 (via A).
- B tells A: "C is at distance 3". A updates its route: C = 4 (via B).
- A tells B: C = 4, so B updates C = 5.
- This continues: 6, 7, 8, ... each update adds 1. The costs count upward toward infinity (RIP defines infinity as 16), and packets for C loop between A and B meanwhile.

Split horizon: a router does not advertise a route back out of the interface from which it learned it. A learned C through B, so A does not tell B about C. After the failure, B hears nothing about C from A, so it marks C unreachable. The loop between two routers is prevented. With poison reverse A would send B the route "C = infinity", which makes this even faster.

It does not solve everything. In topologies with three or more routers in a loop, the wrong route can still travel around the loop. Other fixes are hold-down timers and triggered updates, and link-state protocols such as OSPF avoid the problem altogether.

answers.author: Vikram Sandhu
answers.body:
The key sentence for the exam: distance vector routers only know what their neighbours tell them, not the path behind the number, so they cannot detect that a neighbour's route goes through themselves. Bad news travels slowly (one hop per update) while good news travels fast.

A numerical example helps in the exam: with RIP the maximum metric is 16, so the count stops when the cost reaches 16 (unreachable). That is why RIP supports networks of at most 15 hops. The count takes many update rounds, each 30 seconds apart, so the loop lasts minutes, which is why triggered updates and hold-down timers were added.

doubts.subject: CN
doubts.author: Yash Arora
doubts.title: CSMA/CD: how is the minimum frame size related to the propagation delay?
doubts.body: Question: a 10 Mbps Ethernet LAN has a maximum length such that the round trip propagation time is 51.2 microseconds. Why is the minimum frame size 64 bytes? I understand collision detection in words but I cannot link it to the formula Tt >= 2 x Tp. What does the sender need to be doing for the whole time? And what changes if the bandwidth becomes 100 Mbps?

answers.author: Priya Nair
answers.body:
In CSMA/CD the sender must still be transmitting when the collision signal reaches it. Otherwise it will think the frame was sent successfully and never detect the collision.

Worst case: station A is at one end and station B at the other, with propagation delay Tp between them. A starts sending. Just before the signal reaches B (almost Tp later), B starts sending and immediately sees a collision. B's jam signal then needs another Tp to travel back to A. So A learns about the collision after about 2 x Tp. A must keep transmitting until then, so the transmission time of the frame must be at least the round-trip time:

Tt >= 2 x Tp, which means L / B >= 2 x Tp, so L_min = 2 x Tp x B.

With B = 10 Mbps and 2 x Tp = 51.2 microseconds:
L_min = 10 x 10^6 x 51.2 x 10^-6 = 512 bits = 64 bytes.

That 51.2 microseconds is the slot time of classic Ethernet.

At 100 Mbps with the same minimum frame of 64 bytes, the frame is sent 10 times faster, so the network diameter must shrink to a tenth (about 205 m for Fast Ethernet). Alternatively, you keep the same diameter and increase the minimum frame size to 640 bytes. Real Fast Ethernet kept 64 bytes and reduced the maximum cable length.

answers.author: Tanvi Rao
Zoya Khan

If you really do have several threads, use CopyOnWriteArrayList or a concurrent collection from java.util.concurrent. doubts.subject: OOPJ
doubts.author: Aditya Bansal
doubts.title: Method overriding vs overloading: why does the child's method run through a parent reference?

answers.author: Tanvi Rao
answers.body:
Java decides which overridden method to run at runtime, based on the actual object type, not the reference type. This is runtime polymorphism (dynamic method dispatch). The reference type `Animal` only decides what you are allowed to call at compile time (`a.sound()` is allowed because Animal has sound()). The object created with `new Dog()` decides which implementation executes, which is Dog's.

Overriding vs overloading:
- Overriding: a subclass provides a new implementation of an inherited method with the same name and parameter list (and a compatible return type, and no weaker access). Resolved at RUNTIME.
- Overloading: several methods in the same class with the same name but different parameters. Resolved at COMPILE TIME using the declared types of the arguments.

Variables and static methods do not behave polymorphically:

```java
class A { String name = "A"; static void hi() { System.out.println("A"); } }
class B extends A { String name = "B"; static void hi() { System.out.println("B"); } }
A x = new B();
System.out.println(x.name);  // A  (fields use the reference type)
x.hi();                      // A  (static methods are hidden, not overridden)
```

Add @Override to the subclass method. The compiler then reports an error if you accidentally overload instead of override, for example by changing a parameter type.

answers.author: Zoya Khan
answers.body:
Private, final and static methods cannot be overridden, so they are bound at compile time. A private method in the parent is not even visible to the child, so a method with the same name in the child is a brand new method.

To remember it: overriding needs inheritance and an identical signature, and the JVM picks the method at runtime using the object's real class. Overloading needs only the same name in one class with different parameter lists, and the compiler picks it. A common viva trap is f(Object o) versus f(String s) called with null; the more specific String version is chosen.

doubts.subject: OOPJ
doubts.author: Pooja Saini
doubts.title: Abstract class or interface? When should I use which in Java 8 and later?
doubts.body: Since Java 8 interfaces can have default and static methods. Then I do not understand what is left as a difference between an abstract class and an interface. In the viva I said "interface has only abstract methods" and was told this is outdated. Can someone explain the real differences and when to prefer one over the other, with an example?

answers.author: Zoya Khan
answers.body:
Real differences today:

| | Abstract class | Interface |
|---|---|---|
| Inheritance | A class extends only ONE | A class can implement MANY |
| State | Can have instance fields, constructors | Only constants (public static final), no constructors |
| Methods | Any access level, abstract or concrete | public; abstract, default, static or private (Java 9+) |
| Purpose | Share code and state in a family of classes | Define a capability / contract |

When to choose:
- Use an abstract class when subclasses are closely related and share fields or common code: `abstract class Shape { String color; abstract double area(); }`.
- Use an interface when unrelated classes should be usable in the same way (Comparable, Runnable, Serializable), or when you need multiple inheritance of type.
- Prefer interfaces for APIs; default methods let you add new behaviour without breaking existing implementers.

Default method conflict: if a class implements two interfaces with the same default method, you must override it and can choose one with `InterfaceName.super.method()`.

A good rule: "is-a" with shared state means abstract class; "can-do" means interface.

answers.author: Rohan Mehta
answers.body:
An extra point worth knowing for the exam: an interface can extend several other interfaces, and a class can both extend an abstract class and implement interfaces at the same time. A common design is an interface for the contract plus an abstract class that provides a skeleton implementation, like List and AbstractList in the JDK.

Since Java 8 you also see functional interfaces, which are interfaces with exactly one abstract method such as Runnable or Comparator. They can be used with lambda expressions, which an abstract class cannot. That is one more practical reason to prefer interfaces for small behaviours that you want to pass around as arguments.
