doubts.author: Kabir Sethi
doubts.title: Probability of at least one six in four rolls of a die
doubts.body: Problem from the tutorial: a fair die is rolled 4 times. What is the probability of getting at least one six? I tried adding 1/6 four times, which gives 4/6, but that cannot be right since the answer should not depend on adding like that. My friend said to find the probability of no six and subtract from 1. I do not see why this is easier. Can someone explain properly?

answers.author: Navya Iyer
answers.body:
Adding 1/6 four times double counts. The events "six on roll 1" and "six on roll 2" can both happen, and the sum counts those outcomes more than once. You would also get a probability above 1 for 7 rolls (7/6), which is impossible.

The complement trick is easier because "at least one six" has many cases (exactly one, two, three or four sixes), but its opposite has just one case: no six at all.

- P(no six on one roll) = 5/6.
- The rolls are independent, so P(no six in 4 rolls) = (5/6)^4 = 625/1296.
- P(at least one six) = 1 - 625/1296 = 671/1296, which is about 0.5177.

So the chance is slightly more than half. This is a classic problem, and it explains why a gambler betting "a six in four rolls" wins slightly more than half the time.

General pattern: P(at least one) = 1 - P(none). Use it whenever the problem says "at least" or "one or more".

answers.author: Sneha Pillai
answers.body:
Check with the direct method for a smaller case, two rolls. Exactly one six: 2 x (1/6)(5/6) = 10/36. Two sixes: 1/36. Sum = 11/36. The complement gives 1 - 25/36 = 11/36, the same answer with much less work.

Another check with the general formula: for n rolls the probability of at least one six is 1 - (5/6)^n. For n = 1 it is 1/6, for n = 4 it is 0.518 and for n = 13 it is 0.906. The value rises steadily towards 1 but never reaches it. Plotting these few values makes the pattern easy to remember.

doubts.subject: MATH
doubts.author: Manav Jindal
doubts.title: How many ways can 5 people sit around a circular table? Why do we divide by n?
doubts.body: In the combinatorics tutorial the answer for arranging 5 people around a round table is 4! = 24, but for a straight row it is 5! = 120. I do not understand where the 24 comes from. Rotating everyone one seat gives the same arrangement, I get that, but how does this lead to 4!? Also what changes if the table has a head, or if clockwise and anticlockwise arrangements are treated as the same, like beads on a necklace?

answers.author: Aanya Sharma
answers.body:
Count the arrangements in a row first: 5! = 120. In a circle, an arrangement and its rotations count as the same seating. For 5 people there are exactly 5 rotations of any arrangement (shift everyone by 0, 1, 2, 3 or 4 seats), and all 5 are the same circular arrangement. So every circular arrangement was counted 5 times in the 120:

Circular arrangements = 5! / 5 = 4! = 24.

Another way to see it: fix one person (say A) at a particular seat to remove the rotation. The other 4 people can then be arranged in the remaining 4 seats in 4! = 24 ways.

In general, n people around a table: (n - 1)!.

Variations:
- Clockwise and anticlockwise treated as the same (a necklace or bracelet, no distinction between a pattern and its mirror image): divide by 2 again, so (n - 1)! / 2 for n >= 3. For 5 beads that is 12.
- A table with a head or numbered seats: now rotations are different, so the answer is back to n! = 120.
- Two particular people must sit together: treat them as one block, giving (n - 2)! circular arrangements of 4 units... which is 3! = 6, times 2 for the order inside the block = 12.

doubts.subject: MATH
doubts.author: Aditya Bansal
doubts.title: Prove 1 + 2 + ... + n = n(n+1)/2 by induction: stuck in the inductive step
doubts.body: We have to prove by mathematical induction that the sum of the first n natural numbers is n(n+1)/2. I did the base case n = 1 (1 = 1 x 2 / 2, fine). In the inductive step I assume P(k) is true and need to show P(k+1). I write the left side for k+1 but I do not know how to use the assumption and I end up going in circles. How should I structure the step?

answers.author: Aanya Sharma
answers.body:
Structure of an induction proof: base case, inductive hypothesis, inductive step, conclusion.

Claim P(n): 1 + 2 + ... + n = n(n+1)/2.

Base case: for n = 1, the left side is 1 and the right side is 1 x 2 / 2 = 1. True.

Inductive hypothesis: assume P(k) is true for some k >= 1, that is 1 + 2 + ... + k = k(k+1)/2.

Inductive step: we must show P(k+1): 1 + 2 + ... + k + (k+1) = (k+1)(k+2)/2.

Start from the left side and split off the last term so the assumption can be used:

1 + 2 + ... + k + (k+1) = [1 + 2 + ... + k] + (k+1)
= k(k+1)/2 + (k+1)    (using the hypothesis)
= (k+1)(k/2 + 1)
= (k+1)(k+2)/2.

This is exactly the right side of P(k+1).

Conclusion: P(1) is true and P(k) implies P(k+1), so by the principle of mathematical induction P(n) holds for all n >= 1.

The trick you were missing: write the (k+1) sum as "the k sum plus one more term". That is where the hypothesis enters.

answers.author: Ira Kapoor
answers.body:
Common mistake to avoid: never start from the formula you want to prove and work both sides toward each other, as if it were already true. Start from one side only and transform it into the other, as shown above. Write "by the inductive hypothesis" at the line where you use it, because examiners look for that phrase.

For practice, prove that the sum of the first n odd numbers equals n squared with the same structure: the base case n = 1 gives 1, and the inductive step adds the next odd number 2k + 1 to k squared to get (k + 1) squared.

doubts.subject: MATH
doubts.author: Gurnoor Dhillon
doubts.title: Handshaking lemma: why is the sum of degrees always even?
doubts.body: Our teacher stated the handshaking lemma: the sum of the degrees of all vertices in a graph equals twice the number of edges. I can see it works for the examples I draw, but I would like to understand why. Also, a question asked: can a graph have 7 vertices each of degree 3? I guessed yes but the answer is no, and I cannot connect it to the lemma.

answers.author: Navya Iyer
answers.body:
Why the sum is 2 x edges: every edge connects two vertices, so it adds 1 to the degree of each of its two endpoints. If you add up all the degrees, each edge has been counted exactly twice, once at each end.

Sum of deg(v) over all vertices = 2|E|.

(A self-loop adds 2 to the degree of its vertex, so the formula still holds.)

Consequence: the sum of degrees equals 2|E|, which is an even number. Even numbers have an even count of odd terms, so the number of vertices with odd degree is always even.

Your question: 7 vertices each of degree 3 would give a degree sum of 7 x 3 = 21, which is odd. But the sum must be 2|E|, which is even. So such a graph cannot exist. (Equivalently, 7 vertices of odd degree is an odd number of odd-degree vertices.)

Compare: 6 vertices of degree 3 is possible, for example the complete bipartite graph K(3,3), with 9 edges, since 6 x 3 = 18 = 2 x 9.

answers.author: Sneha Pillai
answers.body:
This is useful in real life too: at a party, the number of people who shook hands an odd number of times is always even. That is the origin of the name. Try it on any small group to convince yourself.

Another consequence: the number of vertices with odd degree is always even, so a degree sequence like 3, 3, 3, 2, 2 (three odd entries) is impossible, while 3, 3, 3, 3, 2 is fine. Checking the parity of the degree sum is the fastest way to reject an impossible degree sequence in a question, before trying to draw anything.

doubts.subject: MATH
doubts.author: Manav Jindal
doubts.title: How to check reflexive, symmetric and transitive from a relation matrix?
doubts.body: I am given a relation on the set {1, 2, 3} as a 3x3 matrix of 0s and 1s. The questions say "is it reflexive, symmetric, transitive?". I know the definitions in words but when I look at a matrix I do not know what to check. For transitive I try all combinations and it takes me a long time. Is there a quicker way using the matrix?

hints.content: Translate each definition into a statement about positions in the matrix. For example, "every element is related to itself" means something about the diagonal. What would symmetric mean for the entry in row i, column j versus row j, column i?

**Approach**
- Reflexive: check the main diagonal; all entries must be 1.
- Symmetric: compare the matrix with its transpose; entry (i, j) must equal entry (j, i) for every pair.
- Transitive: compute the boolean square of the matrix (M times M, with OR for addition and AND for multiplication) and check that every 1 in M squared is also a 1 in M.
- Antisymmetric: for i different from j, entries (i, j) and (j, i) are never both 1.
- Pitfall: transitivity needs every chain a to b to c, including cases where a equals c.

doubts.subject: MATH
doubts.author: Kabir Sethi
doubts.title: Solve T(n) = 2T(n/2) + n using the recurrence tree method
doubts.body: I am learning recurrences for the algorithms course. The recurrence for merge sort is T(n) = 2T(n/2) + n and the book says T(n) = Theta(n log n). I do not understand how to get this from a recursion tree. How many levels are there, what is the cost of each level and how do I add them up? I also want to know how the same method changes for T(n) = 2T(n/2) + 1.

answers.author: Sneha Pillai
answers.body:
Draw the recursion tree and compute the cost level by level.

- Level 0: one problem of size n. Work at this level: n.
- Level 1: two problems of size n/2. Work: 2 x (n/2) = n.
- Level 2: four problems of size n/4. Work: 4 x (n/4) = n.
- Level i: 2^i problems of size n/2^i. Work: 2^i x (n/2^i) = n.

Every level costs n in total.

Number of levels: the size becomes 1 when n / 2^i = 1, so i = log2(n). There are log2(n) + 1 levels, counting the leaves.

Total = n x (number of levels) = n log2(n) + n, which is Theta(n log n).

The leaves: there are 2^(log2 n) = n leaves, each costing T(1) = constant, so that adds Theta(n), which is dominated by the n log n term.

For T(n) = 2T(n/2) + 1: the level costs are 1, 2, 4, ..., 2^i, which is a geometric series. The last level has n leaves, and the sum is about 1 + 2 + 4 + ... + n = 2n - 1 = Theta(n). Here the cost grows going down the tree, so the leaves dominate. In the merge sort case every level costs the same, so you multiply by the height.
